title: Lucky Thread
idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into his hems for luck. Now, every Dior piece that returns to the atelier for repair or restyling is finished with a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in the lining. It is never sold, only earned by keeping a piece alive. Wear becomes a badge of devotion instead of a flaw, and the artisan who did the mending is credited by name. The ritual runs across boutiques, the runway, social content, resale and the archive. It starts with couture and iconic lines to protect quality, and pieces beyond repair are reborn as atelier reinterpretations or archival keepsakes. Dior doesn't preach about sustainability. It makes keeping a piece the most luxurious thing a client can do.
follow_up_questions: How could the sprig change the way a piece is valued in resale, and how can Dior encourage that without commercialising a mark that must stay unbuyable? | Which touchpoints, such as the boutique handover, the artisan's note or a runway moment, would make receiving a repaired piece feel like an event? | How might the atelier scale its capacity and keep hand-finished quality as the ritual expands beyond couture and iconic lines?

title: Owe Me One
idea: Every payment app makes it easy to settle up and never see each other again. Owe Me One adds a different option to the split-the-bill or covered-coffee moment: 'Settle in person.' Instead of sending money, you say 'I'll get you back,' and the app proposes a shared date. The money stays ready as a fallback if the plan falls through, with no guilt. A payments brand choosing not to complete a transaction is the provocation: time with people is the one currency that can't be sent digitally. It launches as a pilot with a P2P partner and host cafes, and grows through content and social asking 'Who do you owe one?' Nobody is labelled lonely. Everyone just has someone to see.
follow_up_questions: What other small, everyday social debts (a borrowed book, a favour, a lift) could become reasons to reconnect, and could the platform stretch beyond money? | How would the mechanic need to change to feel natural for different relationships, such as old friends, colleagues, and family across distance? | What would count as proof that the idea reduces isolation (meetups completed, repeat meetings, friendships revived), and how could Mastercard share it without compromising user privacy?

title: Frame the First One
idea: Direct deposit turned a milestone you once held in your hands into a quiet number in an app. Canva brings the ritual back with a 'First Paycheck' keepsake: a check-style artifact showing the date, the job, what you did that week, who you told first, and an amount you can hide. The number is private; the milestone isn't. Share it, or print and frame it with Canva Print. Freelancers get a 'first paid' version, and employers can send new hires a team-signed one, giving Canva for Teams a human way into onboarding. Real stories of first jobs, told with no promises about hiring, give the launch its voice. The tone is 'your first one, however it went', so it welcomes everyone.
follow_up_questions: What small physical detail (a perforated stub, a signature line, a handwritten note) would make the keepsake feel like an object people want to keep, and not just a graphic they post? | What would make an employer-signed keepsake something a new hire actually values, and how might it work for first jobs that are part-time, temporary or unhappy? | If this became a yearly ritual, who would own it: the person receiving the first paycheck, the people who helped them get there, or the workplaces that hand it over?

title: The Payslip, Redesigned
idea: The first paycheck is thrilling until you open the payslip and can't read it. Canva redesigns it so it explains itself: a plain-language, visual 'where did my money go' page that doubles as a keepsake. Launch with a before-and-after reveal of real, redacted first payslips, and let anyone restyle and share their own, with the numbers hidden and an optional thank-you to whoever helped them get there. Employers and payroll providers adopt the same design through Canva for Teams templates, starting with a small pilot. Each line is explained, never advised. It starts with the payslip and grows into tax, benefits and pension statements: Canva making the confusing clear.
follow_up_questions: What is the single before-and-after image that would make someone stop scrolling, and whose real first payslip should it be? | Which first employers or payroll providers would gain the most from pioneering this, and what would make it an easy yes for them? | After the payslip, which other confusing document in working life would benefit most from this treatment, and who would want to share it?

title: First Paid
idea: Nobody remembers the amount on their first paycheck, but everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck. First Paid invites people to publish a receipt that pairs that first paid creation with a date and, if they choose, who paid them. The amount is blurred by default. Creators and well-known figures seed the gallery before launch. Starter templates, including a First Invoice, cover freelancers, employees, students and founders, and a thank-you tag lets people send their receipt to the person who paid them. Employers can mark a new hire's first paid work with a team version. Later, the gallery reveals the most common first paid work in each city. 'Made in Canva' becomes a badge of a career beginning.
follow_up_questions: What would make someone proud enough to publish their first paid work even if it looks amateur today, and how could the format celebrate that rather than hide it? | Which first-payer stories (a parent, a neighbor, a boss, a stranger online) are most surprising, and could each become its own chapter of the campaign? | How might the receipt idea adapt to cultures where first earnings are private, shared with family, or marked by ritual, and what local versions would feel natural?

title: The New Look, Again
idea: In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For the New Look's 80th anniversary, it answers abundance with what already exists. Dior invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, with its story. The atelier remakes a selection into couture, filmed from first cut to final fitting, each piece carrying an optional signature stitch and a record of its story. A few non-Dior garments are welcome. The anniversary show closes with the remade pieces worn by their original owners. On the same day, boutiques launch a Dior repair and alteration service, so the couture is the showcase, not the whole offer. Short atelier films show the hands behind it all.
follow_up_questions: Which kinds of garments and stories (a mother's jacket, a wedding dress, a worn-out favourite) would make the public most want to submit, and how should the selection be curated to avoid favouring only the glamorous? | What would the boutique repair tier need to offer in price, speed and experience for a client to choose it over buying new? | How should the remade pieces live after the show (exhibition, archive, back with their owners), and who should decide?

title: Tap Together
idea: Loneliness rarely says its name, and asking for company feels risky. Tap Together turns the invitation into generosity. Anyone can send a friend, neighbour, former colleague or relative an 'on me' invitation to a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles at a local business. It only unlocks when both cards tap at the same terminal during the same visit, so the treat can't be consumed alone. The sender takes the social risk, and the receiver can say yes without confessing anything. Unused invitations return to the sender. Participating merchants carry a window mark and a slower, lingering version of the Mastercard sound. Mastercard's most familiar gesture, the tap, becomes a sign of showing up for someone. Success is measured in shared visits, not invitations sent.
follow_up_questions: Who is the most powerful first sender: a charity, a creator, an employer, or an ordinary person who remembers someone they've lost touch with? | What would make the invitation feel like a warm human gesture rather than a transaction, in its wording, timing and the moment of the tap? | How could the idea reach people who would never open an app or accept help, and who might be the trusted messenger in their community?

title: The New Look, Again
idea: In 1947, Dior reshaped fashion by reimagining what already existed. Now, each season, the ateliers invite clients to bring a treasured piece from any year: a tired Bar jacket, a worn Lady Dior, an inherited coat. The petites mains re-cut, repair and reinterpret it into the season's silhouette. Chosen pieces walk the runway and star in a film series that names the artisans and tells each owner's story. Every transformed piece carries a lineage record and a small star stitched inside. A permanent atelier repair service keeps the idea alive between seasons, and each season Dior publishes what was kept in use. Reuse becomes the most creative thing a house can do.
follow_up_questions: How could selection be opened up, for example by region, generation or story, so scarcity feels fair rather than exclusive? | Which impact numbers would be most credible to publish each season, and who could verify them independently? | How could the permanent repair service carry the spirit of the seasonal event, so everyday clients feel part of 'the New Look, again'?

title: Take Your Time
idea: Mastercard admits something honest: we helped make paying so fast that, for many people, the last small conversation of the day disappeared. So we bring a minute back. A founding group of independent merchants display a simple counter signal. When a customer chooses to pause their tap, an unhurried version of Mastercard's sonic identity plays, and it means 'no rush here, I've got a minute.' Nobody has to say they're lonely, and nobody is forced to chat. Merchants choose their quiet hours, so queues stay moving. Priceless shrinks from a rare big moment to the smallest, most universal one: a literal minute of someone's time. It travels through sound, signage, merchant pledges and the stories that happen at the till.
follow_up_questions: What would the 'unhurried' sound need to feel like so that people recognise it as an invitation within a second, and what is the right way to let a customer opt in without making it awkward? | Which kinds of merchants and neighbourhoods would make the strongest founding group, and what would they need to gain from taking part beyond goodwill? | How could the idea be extended beyond physical tills, such as to online checkout, delivery or tap on public transport, without losing the human minute at its heart?

title: Overdue
idea: Most of us aren't short of people to call. We're held back by the awkwardness of having left it too long. Overdue borrows the most dreaded piece of financial mail and flips it. You list the friends, relatives and old colleagues you owe a catch-up, and Mastercard sends a mock notice: 'Amount due: one coffee, one catch-up. Overdue by 14 months. No interest charged.' When you both confirm you've met at a local venue, a first-round rebate applies. A call or a walk settles the debt too. You can snooze or forgive any notice. The value is the reunion, not the spend. Only a payments brand could make guilt this warm, and it builds into Overdue Day, 'paid in full' stories and workplace editions.
follow_up_questions: What other pieces of financial language or paperwork, such as statements, receipts, interest or credit, could be flipped to make a hard emotional step feel easier? | Who is the 'debt' hardest to settle with: an estranged family member, a friend who moved away, a former colleague? Would a different tone or mechanic suit each? | How could the idea reach people who have no one on their list, or who feel too isolated to send the first message, without turning them into recipients of charity?

title: Take Your Time
idea: Contactless made paying instant, and in doing so quietly removed the last small conversation of many people's day. Mastercard admits it and gives a minute back. Independent shops, cafes and markets display a counter sign saying 'No rush here.' When a customer chooses to pause before tapping, the terminal plays a slower, unhurried version of the Mastercard sound, and the merchant answers with a chat or just a calm moment. Nobody has to say they are lonely, and anyone can join. Starting in quiet hours with a committed group of local merchants, it turns Priceless into a literal minute of someone's time, and it can grow across sound, signage, PR and social.
follow_up_questions: What proof would make merchants feel the unhurried minute is worth their time, and how could Mastercard make taking part easy and rewarding for them? | How could the slower sound and signal be designed so that people instantly recognise it as an invitation, but never feel obliged to chat? | Where else in daily life has speed removed a small human exchange, and could Mastercard give those moments back in the same way?

title: The Cannage Darn
idea: Dior turns repair into a signature. The atelier's petites mains develop a hand-stitched mend based on the cannage lattice, a house code, that owners can choose to show or to hide. A visible mend becomes a mark of a piece that has been loved for years. Each repaired Dior returns with a dated card recording why its owner kept it. The campaign begins with the most-worn heritage pieces, such as the Bar jacket and the Lady Dior, and celebrates them as they are, with their history intact. Mends appear on the runway, in film, in boutiques and in owners' own posts, so one stitch can become a platform. Because it builds on an existing service, it starts credibly and grows in phases as atelier capacity allows.
follow_up_questions: Which Dior pieces carry stories people would be proud to show, and who are the real owners whose decade of wear could become the campaign's first faces? | How could the mend appear in a new collection or on the runway without implying that damage is fashionable, so it still reads as care? | What turnaround time and atelier capacity would make the service feel like a privilege rather than a queue, and how should demand be paced to protect that feeling?

title: First Make, First Pay
idea: Your first paycheck wasn't for showing up. It was for something you made. The campaign invites people to dig out, or rebuild from memory, the first thing they made at work: the shop flyer, the chalkboard menu, the rota, the slide for the boss. Each is paired with what it earned. Canva's keepsake layout sets the artefact beside the pay amount and the date. Handwritten signs and price lists count, and rebuilding from memory is part of the fun. Launch with specific real stories, like '$42 for a menu that sold out of soup.' Then bring it to work: employers get a First Make onboarding kit, where managers share their own first make and new hires create theirs in week one. Every career starts with something you made.
follow_up_questions: Which first makes are surprising enough to lead with (a rota that saved a shift, a hand-painted sign), and who could tell those stories most credibly? | How could the employer chapter feel like a welcome ritual rather than another onboarding task, and which team moments (week one, a first presentation, a first solo project) are the best fit? | Once a pool of first-make stories exists, what is the most natural next chapter: passing a first make on to a current first jobber, a school programme, or something else?

title: Frame the First One
idea: Direct deposit made the first paycheck invisible: a number that appears in an app, with no envelope and no ceremony. Canva gives the ritual back with one signature keepsake, a designed 'First Paycheck' artifact you can make in minutes. It captures the date, the job, what you did that week and who you told first. The amount is hidden by default, because the number is private but the milestone isn't. Share it, print it, frame it. The same format works for teens, graduates, career changers and late starters. Later, employers and teams can send new hires a team-signed version before their first payday, which carries the idea into Canva for Teams without losing its human core.
follow_up_questions: What would make the artifact so visually distinctive that people recognise it at a glance, the way they recognise a polaroid or a boarding pass? | Which other everyday milestones have lost their physical ritual to digital life, and could the same 'make it tangible' approach work for them? | How could the campaign honour people whose first paycheck was complicated, late, small or bittersweet, and make that story feel as worth keeping as the happy ones?

title: Pay, Explained
idea: The first paycheck brings excitement, then deduction shock, then a document nobody can read. Canva redesigns the first payslip so it explains itself: each line gets a plain-language label and a clear visual of where the money went. It doubles as a keepsake. Employers and payroll providers adopt it through Canva for Teams templates, giving HR a better onboarding moment. New earners can restyle their own version with amounts hidden and share it. The before-and-after of a confusing payslip beside a clear one proves Canva's belief that design is clarity, and the platform extends to tax, benefits and pension statements. Explanations stay descriptive, never advisory.
follow_up_questions: Which other confusing documents in working life (offer letters, bonus statements, pension updates) would make the most powerful before-and-after for Canva? | How might HR teams be encouraged to adopt a clearer payslip if it improves new-hire confidence but isn't an obvious cost-saving? | What would make someone proud enough to share their first payslip publicly, and how could the design honour that without exposing personal pay?

title: Line Item: Not in the Job Description
idea: Every first paycheck quietly pays for something nobody hired you to do, and it's often making things look good. The campaign reveals that invisible line item on the pay stub: 'Made the deck everyone ended up presenting.' 'Fixed the menu nobody could read.' It celebrates the accidental designer in every workplace, from cafés to clinics to start-ups, as a skill worth keeping, not a burden. Canva then turns recognition into action with a 'skills receipt' that makes hidden work visible, and a 'make the case for your next paycheck' template for reviews and raise conversations. A manager version lets teams credit this work too. Each new industry, role or career stage becomes a fresh line item, so the idea can keep running.
follow_up_questions: Which first-job line items from industries beyond marketing (retail, care, trades, education) would make people say 'that was me' fastest, and how could you collect them without asking anyone to share pay details? | How could employers and managers become champions of the idea, so that recognising hidden design work feels like a good-management move rather than an admission of unpaid labour? | Beyond the first job, which career moments (first promotion, first team lead, first freelance invoice) could carry the line-item format, and what would the hidden skill be at each stage?

title: The Slow Lane
idea: Mastercard made paying take a fraction of a second. Now it gives time back. In participating local shops and cafés, a marked Slow Lane offers an unhurried counter, a stool, and staff happy to chat. The terminal reads 'Take your time' while the payment still completes instantly. The campaign owns the paradox openly: speed is for when you need it, time is for when you don't. Merchants opt in with a simple kit, no scripts, and no mention of loneliness, so it's for everyone. Local community groups quietly point people towards it, and aggregate Economics Institute footfall data helps choose pilot streets. Success is judged by participation and the conversations it starts, not grand claims.
follow_up_questions: What would make a Slow Lane feel genuinely warm and unforced to a first-time visitor, rather than staged or like a loyalty scheme? | Which everyday places beyond cafés and local shops, such as pharmacies, barbers or market stalls, hold the most untapped human contact, and how could the Slow Lane idea adapt to them? | How might the Slow Lane's signature cues, such as the 'Take your time' terminal message, a sound, or the stool, become recognisable symbols that people want to share and that other brands cannot easily copy?

title: The Second Signature
idea: Dior reframes repair as the moment a piece becomes truly yours. Owners of an iconic Dior piece, starting with the Bar jacket, Saddle bag and Lady Dior, can bring it to the atelier and choose between an invisible mend or a visible one: a hand-stitched 'second signature' in Dior thread, signed by the petite main who made it. The scuff or tear stays part of the story, and the mend makes it a mark of status. Campaign imagery treats wear with the reverence of a runway look: macro photography of stitches and real owners of different ages with their pieces. Access is by waiting list, which keeps the offer exclusive and the atelier workload manageable.
follow_up_questions: What would make a signed mend feel like a status symbol and not a sign of damage, and who are the first people whose pieces should carry it? | How could the second signature evolve into a recognizable Dior code, such as a stitch, a color or a stamp, without becoming a trend item that people want to fake? | How should the atelier's capacity be shared between repairing existing pieces and making new ones so that the waiting list builds desire without frustrating clients?

title: The New Look, Again
idea: Each season, Dior's ateliers invite clients to bring a treasured piece from any year: a tired Bar jacket, a worn Lady Dior, an inherited coat. Selection is open and the criteria are published. The petites mains re-cut, repair and reinterpret each piece into the season's silhouette. The transformed pieces appear on the runway beside the new collection, with their owners credited, and in a film series that tells each piece's story. This echoes the 1947 New Look, which reshaped what already existed. A permanent atelier repair and alteration service keeps the idea going between seasons, and each season Dior publishes verified figures on pieces kept in use, atelier hours and materials reused. Reuse becomes a creative act.
follow_up_questions: What would make a transformed piece feel like a new Dior creation and not a repair, and who should hold the creative pen: the atelier, the creative director or the owner? | How could the permanent repair and alteration service carry the same sense of desire and ceremony as the seasonal event, so that everyday clients feel part of it? | Beyond runway and film, where could these stories reach people who may never own a Dior piece yet still shape what Dior means culturally?

title: The Extra Inch
idea: Inside every well-made Dior couture garment, a hidden inch of seam allowance lets the piece be taken in, let out and re-fitted for decades. The Extra Inch makes that secret visible: Dior's quiet promise that a garment is built to change with the person wearing it. Real owners' refit stories lead the films, with atelier hands doing the work. The inch becomes a unit of measure, a film motif and a booking service for refits, repairs and handovers. For bags and shoes, the 'next inch' means resoling, re-edging and re-strapping. A published Inch Standard backs the claim with real construction rules and atelier capacity. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a single purchase.
follow_up_questions: What would an Inch Standard need to include, and who should verify it, for customers and critics to trust it as proof rather than marketing? | Which moments in a garment's life (a wedding, a pregnancy, a bereavement, a handover to a daughter) would make the strongest refit stories, and how can they be told without feeling exploitative? | How could the 'next inch' idea grow into pre-owned handovers or younger audiences' first Dior piece without weakening the house's exclusivity?

title: Second Fitting
idea: Dior made its name on the first fitting, the moment a garment is made for one body. Second Fitting offers the next one. Any Dior piece, bought new, inherited or found secondhand, can return to the atelier to be re-fitted for the life its owner is living now: a Bar jacket let out for a new body, a mother's coat recut for a daughter, a Lady Dior re-edged. Each piece comes back with a dated, signed label naming the petites mains who worked on it, and an optional star, muguet or bee for those who want the work to show. Real transformations, told through the owners and the hands, become films, boutique salons and a client ledger that makes keeping a Dior piece the ultimate status act.
follow_up_questions: How would the Second Fitting be priced and paced (tiers, waiting times, a visible 'atelier season') so it feels like a privilege and not a repair queue, and what is the honest limit on how many pieces the petites mains can take? | Which present-tense moments of change (a first big job, a new body, a transition, a vintage find) would make a 25-year-old want a Second Fitting as much as an heirloom owner, and who are the real clients who would tell them? | How could the label and ledger grow into a recognised sign of a well-kept piece, for example in how it is worn, passed on or shown, without sliding into a resale platform?

title: Owe Me One
idea: When you split a bill or cover a coffee, a new option appears beside 'Send': Settle in person. Instead of transferring money, you and your friend get a shared date, and a gentle 'I'll get you back' becomes a plan. Mastercard, the brand that made payments instant, deliberately chooses not to finish the transaction, because time with people is the one currency that cannot be sent digitally. If plans fall through, 'Pay now instead' is one tap away. Piloted with a P2P partner and partner cafes, it counts 'debts kept' as real meetups. The social prompt 'Who do you owe one?' invites everyone to name someone they have been meaning to see, with no label and no stigma.
follow_up_questions: What would make someone choose 'Settle in person' over a quick transfer, and when would a small nudge feel like a gift instead of pressure? | Which pilot partner and city would give the most believable proof of 'debts kept', and which meetup stories would make people want to take part? | Beyond friends splitting a bill, where else does a small debt already exist (family, colleagues, neighbours) that could become a reason to meet?

title: Fermé pour réparations
idea: One day a year, Dior closes its flagship on avenue Montaigne to new sales and hangs a sign: Closed for repairs. The shop floor and windows become working ateliers where petites mains mend clients' Dior pieces in public view, including secondhand ones. Boutiques worldwide join in, so the gesture travels around the globe. The most valuable retail space in luxury is given to care instead of newness. The day is the public face of a year-round Dior repair service, launched beforehand and backed by an annual public report on what was mended. It shows craft behind the price and makes repair a house ritual, not a footnote.
follow_up_questions: What should a client leave with after their piece is mended, such as a story, a record of its life or an optional signature detail, so that repair feels like gaining something rather than fixing a loss? | Which year-round commitments would make the closure day credible rather than a stunt, and what would Dior be willing to publish about them each year? | How could the day invite people who do not own Dior, such as secondhand buyers, students or local repairers, without diluting the sense of luxury?

title: First Stub: the most important document at work finally makes sense
idea: Your first pay stub is the first proof that your work counts, and it's usually a grey grid nobody can read. Canva redesigns it into a clear, human one-page story: hours as a visual timeline, deductions in plain language, and space for a personal welcome note from the team. It ships as a free template kit that HR teams customise and send with the first pay, with integration-ready layouts for payroll and HR platforms. Presentation only: no tax or financial advice, and payroll accuracy stays with the employer's provider. The hero film follows a first-time earner comparing the old stub with the new one. Payday add-ons include a thank-you stub for new hires to send to the person who helped them, and the kit later grows to offer letters, benefits sheets and onboarding packs.
follow_up_questions: Which first-job moment would make the strongest hero film: a teenager's summer job, a graduate's first salary, or someone starting again after a career change? | Which payroll or HR platforms would make the best launch partners, and what would they need to see to co-develop integration-ready layouts? | How far can plain-language labelling go before it starts to sound like advice, and who (legal, payroll partners, HR experts) should help set that line?

title: Paid For This
idea: Everyone remembers their first paycheck, but the real story is what it paid for: the menu you typed up, the pitch deck you stayed late on, the flyer for a Saturday shift, the logo for a friend's café. 'Paid For This' flips the payslip photo. People post their first piece of paid work, with the amount hidden by default, and add the feeling or story behind it. A Canva template makes sharing easy, but any first job counts. Real creators, interns and small-business owners seed it, then it travels through OOH showing real first work and into employer and school onboarding. The paycheck becomes proof of ability, not salary, and Canva becomes the place where work worth being paid for gets made.
follow_up_questions: Which first jobs or kinds of first work would feel least obvious for Canva, and how could the format still make them feel central? | How could employers, schools or small-business networks use 'Paid For This' to welcome new starters without it feeling like a corporate culture exercise? | What would make people return to the idea after the first wave, such as a 'Paid For This, again' format for later milestones like a first promotion or a first client?

title: Overdue
idea: Nobody dreads a bill like an overdue notice, so Mastercard borrows one for something better. People list the friends, relatives and old colleagues they owe a catch-up, and receive a mock notice: 'Amount due: one coffee, one catch-up. Overdue by 14 months.' Settle it by meeting at a local venue and tapping your own Mastercard, and the first round is on us. Prefer a call or a walk? That settles it too, and any debt can be snoozed or forgiven. Loneliness charities help shape the tone and receive unclaimed rebates. Participating venues host an 'Overdue table', and an annual Overdue Day and workplace editions keep it going. The value is the reunion, not the spend.
follow_up_questions: What is the funniest or most touching way to make 'paid in full' feel like a real emotional release, for the people involved and for those watching their stories? | Who might be left out when the hook is a debt owed to friends (people who have no one on their list), and what would a warm, non-patronising route in look like? | Beyond coffee with friends, which other overdue things could this language of bills and balances reach, such as apologies, thank-yous, family visits or neighbours?

title: The Second Signature
idea: Dior turns repair into a mark of status. When an owner brings back a loved Bar jacket, Saddle bag or Lady Dior, they choose an invisible mend or a signed one: a hand-stitched Dior gesture in thread, finished with a small atelier mark and the name of the petite main who made it. The mend becomes a second signature, proof that a piece was worn, loved and kept in the maison's own hands. Resale platforms and third-party menders cannot offer it. Campaign imagery treats the mend with runway reverence, through macro photography, editorials and real owner stories. Launching as a waitlisted capsule of icons keeps it exclusive and operationally manageable.
follow_up_questions: What would make a signed mend feel earned rather than bought, and should the mark be tied to how long a piece has been loved or worn? | How could the second signature spread beyond Dior's own clients, for example through creative directors, ambassadors or archive pieces wearing visible mends, without becoming a trend that cheapens it? | Where is the line between honoring a piece's history and romanticizing damage, and how should the campaign's tone and imagery stay on the right side of it?

title: The Covered Invite
idea: People don't only stop going out. They stop inviting, because of cost and the fear of being a burden. The Covered Invite removes both. Any cardholder can send a digital invitation to a coffee, a meal or a class, and Mastercard covers the guest's first item at participating local merchants. The message is simple: 'It's covered. Just come.' Invitations can be themed for a new neighbour, an old friend, a colleague or 'first one back', and can peak in the holidays. Merchants gain off-peak footfall and become 'regular' places where guests can be known. Caps, fraud controls and a phased launch keep it sustainable. Priceless becomes a working mechanism: Mastercard pays for the seat, people supply the moment.
follow_up_questions: Who is the one person you have stopped inviting, and what would make you send that invitation tomorrow? | What would make an invitation feel like a personal gesture rather than a promotion, and how could the creative and the invite itself show that? | Beyond a first coffee, what could turn a single covered invite into a regular habit, and who else (merchants, employers, communities) should help make that happen?

title: Line Item: Not in the Job Description
idea: Every first paycheck quietly pays for something nobody hired you to do, and it's often making things look good. The campaign adds the invisible line item to a stylised first pay stub: 'Designing the thing nobody else wanted to design.' People across teachers, nurses, retail, trades and operations add their own line items, which creates a repeatable, shareable format. Canva then turns recognition into action with a 'skills receipt' and a 'make the case for your next paycheck' template, plus a manager version that names and backs the hidden skill. Design becomes an everyday work skill, and Canva becomes the workplace tool for the accidental designer.
follow_up_questions: Which line items would be most surprising and true for non-creative roles, and how could you collect them without the campaign feeling like it belongs only to marketers? | How could managers and employers join in as champions of the hidden skill, so the idea sells Teams and Enterprise without sounding like a complaint about unpaid work? | Beyond the first job, which career moments (first promotion, first team lead, first freelance invoice) could become new editions of the Line Item format?

title: The New Look, Again
idea: In 1947, Dior answered scarcity with abundance. For the New Look's 80th anniversary, it answers abundance with what already exists. Dior invites people to submit a garment they cannot let go of, along with its story. The atelier remakes a selection into couture pieces, filmed from first cut to final fitting, and the anniversary show closes with the owners wearing them. Each remake carries a discreet Dior repair mark and a provenance record. On the same day, boutiques launch a repair and alteration service for every Dior owner, so reuse reaches beyond couture. The idea says that the most radical luxury is the piece you already love.
follow_up_questions: What would make a person choose to repair a Dior piece they own rather than buy a new one, and how could the campaign speak to that moment? | How could the stories of the submitted garments reach people who have never owned Dior, without the campaign feeling out of reach? | What should happen to the remade pieces and their owners after the show, so the idea continues beyond the anniversary?

title: The Slow Lane
idea: Mastercard made paying take a fraction of a second. Now it gives some time back. Local cafés, bakeries and shops opt in to offer a Slow Lane: a signposted spot at the till with no queue pressure, a stool if there's room, and staff glad to chat. The terminal still completes the payment instantly, but the screen says 'Take your time.' It's for everyone, so nobody has to say they're lonely to use it. Mastercard owns its part in the speed story and uses it to back small businesses and the human moments around a purchase. A pilot on a few streets, with a simple merchant kit and local charity partners, can grow into a wider programme.
follow_up_questions: What would make a shop owner feel the Slow Lane is a genuine asset to their business, not an extra burden on a busy day? | How could the Slow Lane feel warm and welcoming without staff or customers feeling pressured to talk, so that quiet company counts as success too? | Beyond the till, where else has Mastercard's drive for speed removed a small human moment, and could a 'slow' option work there as well?

title: Paid For This
idea: Everyone remembers their first paycheck, but the real story is what it paid for. Paid For This flips the payslip photo: people share their first piece of paid work, whether a menu, a pitch deck, a flyer, a logo or a shift rota, with the amount covered by a designed stamp and a feeling or story in its place. A Canva template makes it easy, so pay stays private and the pride goes public. Real creators, small businesses and first bosses seed it, OOH shows genuine first work, and employers and schools hand new starters a card on first payday. Freelancers who share can pick up a first-invoice kit, linking pride to Canva's business tools. The paycheck becomes proof of ability, and Canva becomes the place where work worth paying for gets made.
follow_up_questions: What would the 'stamp' that replaces the amount look like, and could it become a recognisable symbol like a verified badge for first work? | Which employers, schools or small-business communities would be the best early partners for a first-payday card, and what would make them want to use it? | How should the campaign honour first jobs where the work was not visual, such as care, hospitality or manual work, so that they feel as celebrated as a logo or a deck?

title: The Slow Lane
idea: Mastercard made paying faster. Now it says: not everything should be. The Slow Lane turns one checkout lane in partner grocers, pharmacies and markets into an unhurried one, marked 'This lane takes its time.' Cashiers opt in, are given the time to talk, and are recognised for it. An optional Slow Tap mode on Mastercard's own terminal swaps the efficient beep for a warmer pause. The lane is open to anyone, so no one has to admit to being lonely. Mastercard funds an off-peak pilot, publishes the results on throughput, cashier experience and customer wellbeing, and grows it into Slow Hour and a sonic signature only if the evidence holds. A payments giant arguing for slowness earns attention, and making the cashier the hero keeps it from being a stunt.
follow_up_questions: What would cashiers need (protected time, recognition, pay, training, the right to opt out) to see the Slow Lane as a source of pride and not extra work? | Where else has speed quietly removed the last human exchange of someone's day (self-checkout, pharmacy counters, ticket desks, bank branches), and which of Mastercard's assets could slow those moments down? | What would a 'slow' sound or gesture at the terminal feel like so that people notice and talk about it without feeling singled out?

title: It's Covered
idea: People don't only stop going out; they stop asking, because asking feels costly and like a burden. Mastercard lets any cardholder send a digital invitation to a coffee, meal or class with a simple promise: 'It's covered. Just come.' Mastercard pays for the guest's first item at participating local merchants, where owners and long-time regulars are ready to welcome newcomers. Ready-made themes (new neighbour, old friend, first one back) make the first message easy, and guests can reply privately with no obligation, then pass on an invite of their own. Launching in a few markets with caps and fraud controls, it turns Priceless into a working mechanism, brings off-peak footfall to small businesses, and is measured by invites sent, accepted and redeemed.
follow_up_questions: Which moments of life (moving to a new city, retirement, a break-up, returning to work) are the most powerful first themes for invitations, and how would each change the tone? | How could the invitation itself become a shareable, beautiful object that people are proud to send, without turning loneliness into something people have to announce? | What would make a small merchant feel like a co-author of the idea, rather than a redemption point, and what could they offer beyond the first item?

title: Pay Together
idea: Money that only works when two people are together. Someone sends a small 'Together' gift, such as a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles, as a virtual Mastercard. It unlocks only when both phones tap at the same independent local venue. The payment is the invitation, so nobody has to ask 'do you want to hang out?'. For people with no one to send it to, Open Tap works with befriending charities and community groups to arrange gifts and gentle introductions. Gifts stay small, venues stay unbranded and welcoming, and success is counted in meetings made, not money spent. Start in one city, with pilot areas chosen using aggregate insight, and let the stories spread from there.
follow_up_questions: What is the smallest gift value and the most ordinary venue that would still make someone say yes, and how would you find out? | Beyond befriending charities, which unexpected partners (employers, universities, GP surgeries, new-parent groups, landlords) could turn Open Tap into a front door for people who have no one to invite? | What would a second Together meeting look like, and how could the idea support the step from a one-off coffee to a lasting habit without becoming a loyalty scheme?

title: The Paycheck, Explained
idea: The first paycheck is a milestone that arrives as a confusing document. Canva redesigns it. Launch with ugly, dense, fictional pay stubs in public places and on social, then reveal the Canva makeover: gross-to-net turned into a clear, friendly visual story with a plain-language jargon legend. Free templates let first-timers decode their stub and let HR teams and small business owners hand new hires a clear explainer plus a short welcome note. Everything uses fictional data and explains rather than advises, with a clear disclaimer. The creative keeps the feeling at the center: the pride and 'wait, where did it go?' of a first real paycheck. Platform: design is how things make sense.
follow_up_questions: Which first-paycheck moment is most universal across jobs and countries: the excitement, the gross-to-net shock, or the first purchase, and which should lead the creative? | How could the redesigned stub work for different pay structures such as hourly, tipped, gig or salaried, without implying financial advice? | What would a later community phase look like that lets people share their paycheck stories safely, without exposing real pay data?

title: The Extra Inch
idea: Inside every well-made Dior couture garment, an extra inch of seam allowance waits, so the piece can be taken in, let out and refitted across decades. The Extra Inch reveals this hidden detail as Dior's quiet promise of a long life, and treats each refit, repair or passing-on as the garment's 'next inch'. Short films follow real owners and the atelier hands who refit their pieces. A bookable Inch Service lets clients refit, repair or pass on a piece, with equivalents like resoling and re-edging for shoes and leather goods. A published longevity standard backs the promise. Luxury becomes a long relationship with a garment, not a single purchase.
follow_up_questions: What would be the most surprising way to let people see or feel the inch, such as a tape measure, a label, a ribbon or a moment of refitting, without a sustainability lecture? | How could the inch work as a promise for pieces with no seam allowance, like bags, shoes and jewellery, so it feels equally true for them? | What should happen at the moment a piece moves to its next owner, and who should get to decide how much of its history is shared?

title: The Cannage Darn
idea: Dior turns repair into a signature. The petites mains develop a hand-stitched mend based on the cannage lattice, and owners choose a visible mark or an invisible one. A visible Cannage Darn becomes a badge of a well-loved piece, and each repaired piece returns with a dated card recording why its owner kept it, a card that can travel with the piece to its next owner. The campaign begins with the Bar jacket and the Lady Dior, launches in a few pop-up salons, and celebrates the most-worn Dior pieces, scuffs and all, as proof of care. The mend then appears on runway, in film, on social and in boutiques, so repair becomes a status gain people want to show.
follow_up_questions: What would make the Cannage Darn feel unmistakably Dior and not like generic visible mending: a particular stitch, thread colour or placement, or a ritual of choosing it? | Who should be the first voices of the campaign: celebrated owners, atelier artisans, or ordinary customers with decades-old pieces, and what story would each tell? | How could the mend show up in new collections and on the runway so that it feels like a creative signature, without turning into a gimmick or pushing people to damage pieces on purpose?

title: The First Thing You Made
idea: Your first paycheck wasn't a reward for showing up. It was payment for the first thing you made: the flyer for the shop, the menu, the rota, the slide the boss needed by Friday. The campaign opens with real stories pairing that first creation with the pay it earned. Anyone can then recreate it, from memory if needed, as a keepsake in Canva, and share it beside their first payday. Handwritten signs and price lists count. For employers, the idea becomes 'First Thing Made Here': a new hire's first-week deliverable celebrated as a welcome ritual. Later chapters can invite veterans to pass on their first creations and start conversations about better work documents. Every career starts with something you made.
follow_up_questions: Which first creations are so specific and surprising (a chalkboard special, a babysitting rota, a lost-cat poster) that they would make people stop and share their own? | How could an employer turn a new hire's first-week deliverable into a ritual that feels earned and not corporate or forced? | If someone made nothing visual in their first job, what other first contributions could count, and how could Canva help them recreate it?

title: Tap Together
idea: Loneliness is hard to admit, so Tap Together lets you invite someone without asking for anything. Send a friend, neighbour, ex-colleague or relative an 'On Me' invitation to a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles at a local business. It only unlocks when both your cards tap at the same terminal during the same visit, so the generosity can't be used alone. The sender takes the social risk; the receiver simply says yes. Warm, ready-made invitation prompts make the first step easy, a distinctive 'together' tap sound marks the moment, and a 'your turn' nudge keeps the chain going. Befriending charities can send invitations for people with no one to ask. Piloted in a few cities, it drives footfall to small businesses and measures success in shared visits.
follow_up_questions: Who is the one person you have been meaning to see for months, and what would make an invitation from them easy to accept? | How could the mechanic reach people who have no one to invite, without turning it into stranger-matching or charity-only territory? | Which moments in the year (a move, a bereavement, retirement, the festive period) would make an 'On Me' invitation feel most natural and least like a promotion?

title: The Slow Lane
idea: Mastercard made paying faster. Now it says: not everything should be. In partner grocers, pharmacies and markets, one checkout lane is marked 'This lane takes its time.' It is open to everyone, whether you want a chat, have no rush, or just like it. Cashiers opt in as paid, recognised Lane Hosts and have the time to talk if they choose. It starts as an off-peak pilot with published results, so merchants see evidence, not a stunt. Because the checkout is often the only conversation an isolated person has all day, the intervention happens where they already are, with no label and no sign-up. If it works, it grows into Slow Hour, Slow Day and a Slow Tap sound, each one a new story for press, merchants and the people in the lane.
follow_up_questions: What other moments of speed or efficiency in your category quietly remove human contact, and could your brand credibly argue for slowing one of them down? | How could a brand make the people who give the time, like cashiers, the stars of the story without turning their kindness into unpaid labour or a marketing prop? | What proof would convince a sceptical merchant or the public that a gesture like this is a lasting commitment, and not a campaign that disappears after a season?

title: Fermé pour réparations
idea: One day a year, Dior closes its flagship to new sales and hangs a sign: Closed for repairs. The shop floor and windows become working ateliers where the petites mains mend clients' own Dior pieces in public view, whether bought new or pre-owned. Boutiques worldwide join in that week. Clients can choose an invisible mend or a discreet tone-on-tone cannage signature, and their stories are told in store and online. The day launches a permanent Dior repair and care service with published commitments, and afterwards Dior reports openly on pieces repaired, materials reused and progress on its supply chain. The house's most valuable space goes to care instead of newness, proving the value of what you already own.
follow_up_questions: What would Dior have to promise publicly, such as turnaround times, lifetime care or pricing, for the repair service to feel like a real offer rather than a one-day gesture? | How could the day be designed so that people who never enter a Dior boutique, including secondhand owners and young fans of vintage Dior, feel invited and not just observers? | Which other luxury rituals, such as a seasonal sale or a store opening, could be inverted in the same way to show care instead of newness, and how might they sit alongside this day as a wider platform?

title: Pay Together
idea: Pay Together is money that only works when two people are in the same place. One person sends a small gift, such as a coffee, a haircut or a bowl of noodles, as a virtual Mastercard in an app. It unlocks only when both people confirm they are together at a local independent venue. The payment is the invitation, so nobody has to say 'I'm lonely, shall we meet?' For people with no one to send a gift to, Open Tap lets befriending charities, neighbourhood groups and new-parent circles give gifts to people who might otherwise stay isolated. Priceless becomes a working mechanism: the gift is worth nothing alone. Pilot it in one city with a few venues and charity partners, and measure meetings made, not money spent.
follow_up_questions: Which moments of life change, such as a move, a new baby, retirement or a new job, make people most hesitant to ask someone to meet, and how could Pay Together appear at exactly those moments? | How could a gift that only works in company be used by workplaces, universities or landlords to welcome newcomers without feeling like forced socialising? | What would make a venue feel like a real host rather than a redemption point, and how could that be built without branding or extra work for small business owners?

title: The Paycheck, Explained
idea: Pay stubs are among the most important and least designed documents in adult life. Canva redesigns the first-paycheck experience, turning the gross-to-net shock into a clear, friendly visual story. First-time earners from retail, kitchens, trades and offices share their 'wait, where did my money go?' moment, then see their sample pay stub made over, using fictional data only. Free templates let HR teams and small business owners explain pay in plain visual language and welcome new hires with a personal note and a team shout-out. OOH mimics ugly pay stubs, then reveals the redesign. The platform is 'Design is how things make sense.' Everything is framed as explanation, not financial advice.
follow_up_questions: Which other 'ugly but important' documents in early adult life (leases, benefits forms, offer letters) could get the same makeover treatment, and how would that widen the platform? | Who is the most credible voice to front the makeovers: first-time earners, payroll or HR professionals, or creators, and how does that choice change the tone? | How could the employer toolkit make HR teams look generous and clear, so that adoption feels like a culture win and not a compliance task?

title: First Paid
idea: Nobody remembers the number on their first paycheck. Everyone remembers what they made to earn it: the bakery menu, the wedding invitation, the first client deck, the logo for a friend's startup. First Paid invites people to publish a receipt for that work: the design itself, the date, and, if they choose, who paid them. The amount stays blurred unless they reveal it. The receipts build into a public gallery of the work that started careers, seeded at launch by creators, Canva staff and familiar names. 'Made in Canva' stops being a watermark and becomes a badge of a beginning. The platform scales through workplace and school activations, local editions, and real stories for B2B proof.
follow_up_questions: What would a 'First Paid' receipt look like in different cultures, where the first paid work and the way people talk about money vary widely? | How could the gallery give something back to the person who paid, such as a thank-you template or a way to tag and reply, so the payer becomes part of the story? | Where could Canva turn these receipts into real-world moments, such as a printed receipt at a graduation, a first-day-at-work desk card, or a wall in a co-working space?

title: First Stub: the human side of work documents
idea: The first pay stub is the most emotional document of early working life, and also the ugliest and least understood. Canva redesigns it into a clear, human one-page story. Hours become a visual timeline, deductions get plain-language labels, and a personal note from the team sits at the top. It ships as a free template kit that employers customise and send with the first pay, with layouts ready for HR and payroll platforms. Canva offers no tax or financial advice, and payroll accuracy stays with the employer. The campaign leads with before/after reveals and first-time earners finally understanding what they earned. It can then grow to offer letters, benefits sheets and onboarding packs, and become the human side of work documents.
follow_up_questions: Which other work document do people remember vividly but find cold or confusing, and what would it look like if it were designed to be understood and felt? | What would make an HR team proud to send a redesigned stub, and how could that pride become a visible employer-brand signal in recruitment? | Where is the line between making a document clearer and implying advice, and how could that line become a trust-building part of the campaign story?

title: Lucky Thread
idea: Christian Dior sewed lily of the valley into hems for luck. Now, every Dior piece brought back to the atelier for repair or restyling is finished with a tiny hand-embroidered muguet sprig in the lining. It can't be bought, licensed or put on merchandise. It can only be earned by keeping a piece alive. Wear becomes a badge, and the artisan who mended it is credited by name in a light lineage record that travels with the piece into resale. The idea launches with artisans stitching the first sprigs in public at 30 Montaigne, appears on mended pieces on the runway, and rolls out from couture and iconic lines to wider ranges. Pieces beyond saving return as a keepsake carrying the sprig.
follow_up_questions: What would make a client feel proud, and not embarrassed, to show the lining of a mended piece, and which moments or rituals could invite that? | How might the credited artisans become recognised figures of the house without the idea tipping into celebrity or overshadowing the pieces? | If the sprig gains value in resale, how can Dior encourage keeping and repairing over trading, so scarcity strengthens devotion and not speculation?

title: Second Fitting
idea: Dior built its name on the first fitting, the moment a garment is made for one body. Second Fitting offers the next one. Any authenticated Dior piece, bought new, inherited or found secondhand, can return to the atelier to be refitted for the life its owner lives now: a Bar jacket let out for a new body, a mother's coat recut for her daughter, a Lady Dior re-edged. Each piece comes back with a dated, signed label naming the petites mains who did the work. The campaign tells real transformations through the people who wear them and the hands that make them, so keeping a Dior piece becomes the ultimate status act.
follow_up_questions: How could Second Fitting feel as relevant to a 25-year-old with a first Dior piece as to a collector with an archive, without leaning on nostalgia? | What is the smallest, most honest version of the service the atelier could deliver reliably at launch, and how would its limits be shown as exclusivity rather than shortcoming? | Beyond the label, what other ritual or object could make a second fitting feel as special as the first, and who should be credited as the heroes of the story?
